headline: Quantum Computer Simulates Matter Forming From Energy
meta_description: Scientists at Duke University used a 13-ion quantum simulator to recreate particle formation, revealing how quantum computers could unlock secrets of the early…
summary_short: Researchers recreated the physics of matter appearing from pure energy using a quantum computer—a breakthrough that could help explain how the universe began.
body:
An international team led by Duke University's Quantum Center has achieved a remarkable milestone: using a quantum computer to simulate particles seemingly "popping into existence" from energy alone. The experiment, published in Nature Physics on September 23, reproduced a phenomenon called string breaking, in which two connected particles are pulled so far apart that their accumulated energy spawns entirely new particles. This process normally requires the extreme conditions of particle colliders or the early moments after the Big Bang itself. By encoding the physics into a chain of 13 trapped ions and manipulating them with precisely controlled laser beams, researchers watched the system evolve and detected the formation of new particles exactly as quantum theory predicts. "Quantum computer simulations provide the best platform to investigate complex questions like matter formation, short of having witnessed the Big Bang itself," said Christopher Monroe, who led the research.

What makes this achievement particularly significant is its breadth. The Duke team verified their results against classical computer models, confirming accuracy. Meanwhile, separate research groups using Google's superconducting circuits and QuEra Computing's neutral atoms achieved similar breakthroughs—suggesting that multiple pathways toward powerful quantum computing are viable. For now, classical computers can still handle simulations at this scale, but as quantum systems grow larger and more complex, they will eventually solve problems that even the world's most powerful supercomputers cannot crack.

The work opens a profound new chapter in physics. Rather than building ever-larger, more expensive particle colliders to study matter's fundamental nature, scientists may soon use quantum computers to safely simulate the universe's deepest mysteries in the laboratory. That shift could reshape how we investigate the cosmos—not by recreating the Big Bang, but by teaching machines to think about it the way nature does.
quick_facts: Duke University led an international collaboration including Oxford, Caltech, and others
Researchers used a chain of 13 trapped ions controlled by laser beams
Experiment simulated string breaking, a process normally requiring extreme particle collider energies
Results validated by classical computer models and confirmed by competing quantum platforms
